en: Om. Salutations to the venerable gurus; salutations to the illustrious Gaṇapati Sundara.
Re 32415 notes:
Words/letters within brackets are my suggestions (to the best of my understanding).
Dots (…) are used to indicate missing portions of the text, such as lost arts, leaf damage, or unidentified characters, occurring mostly at five lines on each side.
*Mannāthasthāpanam* (i.3b).
Ha…… (May there be auspiciousness).
(2) I worship the one who wears a crown and earrings, who has two feet and two hands, who holds a bow and arrow in his hand, and whose face is serene and joyful. (2)
To the one who possesses a hero’s sword, whose weapon has the form of a blow,
who is adorned with a garland of skulls, whose hair stands erect, and who has prominent fangs; salutation to Vināyaka, whose root is like a palm tree.
(i.4a blank) The Installation of the Lord of Men (i.4b): O best of sages, listen as I describe the installation of the Lord of Men.
Specifically in the northeast, at the foremost point of the *ālaya*, one should construct a square sacrificial hall; in its center, two altars (*vedikā*);
and to the east of that, one should have a single square fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) constructed. (2–3)

The eighteen rites, beginning with the worship of Vighneśvara and including the collection of earth, the rite for the site, the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*), and the worship of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), are to be performed as previously described. Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus on the southern altar, one should install [the deity]. One should worship the Lord of the Mantras within the water-pot (*kumbha*).
The visualization (*dhyāna*): "He has one face, four arms, and three eyes, and is well-seated upon a lotus throne. (i.5a)
In his right hand he holds fire, and in his left hand he holds a black deer and displays the gesture of fearlessness.
I worship the form of my Lord, whose feet are supported by Dakṣa as he sleeps, who wears a rosary of Rudrākṣa beads,
whose body is smeared with ashes, and who bears matted locks.
Having meditated thus, one should perform the specific rites beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*).

(3) Having offered the *dhenumudrā*, and having presented the offerings known as food (*naivedya*), incense (*dhūpa*), lamp (*dīpa*), and water for sipping (*ācamana*), one should perform the dedication of the recitation (*japasamarpaṇa*). (4) One should worship the *vardhanī* vessel on the northern side of the main jar (*kumbha*).
One should worship [the deities] in the eight surrounding jars according to the sequence starting from the east. (5)
Having first worshipped Gaṇeśa in the east and Śāstṛ in the southeast...
Having worshipped Brahmā in the south, one should perform the worship of Rudra in the southwest;
[having worshipped Viṣṇu] in the west, and Kṣetrapāla in the northwest.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu in the north and Vīrabhadra in the northeast: (2) "Oṃ gāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Gaṇeśa; obeisance to the form of Gaṇeśa.
[One should meditate on him] as having the color of saffron, endowed with four arms, three faces, a crown, and a *karaṇḍa* box. (3)
Holding a goad, a sweetmeat ball, and a noose in his hands, with eyes like fire, he is the very embodiment of Gaṇanātha.
Homage to Gaṇapati! Having worshipped him, [homage] to the Seat of the Teacher (Śāstāsanāya)! Homage to the Form of the Teacher (Śāstāmūrtaye)!
His body is dark-complexioned and in the full bloom of youth, with locks of hair born from a thousand lotuses on his chest.
[He sits upon] a comfortable lotus-seat encircled by a yoga-band, with his left and right [sides] filled with abundance.
Homage to the Teacher! Having worshipped [him], homage to the Brahmā-throne! Homage to the Form of Brahmā!
Brahmā has four faces, is yellow in color, and is adorned with four staff-like arms. (2)
I worship him who holds a water-pot, a rosary of beads, and a staff of kuśa grass.
Salutation to Brahmā. Jya. (3) Salutation to the seat of Rudra. Salutation to the form of Rudra.
[One should meditate on him] as having three heads, red in color, with matted hair and a crescent moon, four-armed, adorned with serpent ornaments, and possessing three eyes in each face. (4)
One should bear the form of Rudra, holding a spear, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, a garland, and a lotus.
(5) Homage to Rudra! Homage to him whose seat is Guha! Homage to the form of Guha!
[He is] reddish like vermilion, with a face as lovely as the moon, adorned with armlets, necklaces, and other ornaments. (i.6b)
We worship Guha, whose body is adorned with divine ornaments and who bestows the happiness of heaven;
he holds a spear and a cock resembling a lotus, is anointed with red unguents, is Subrahmaṇya, and is ever intent on destroying the fear of those who bow before him. (2–3)
Salutation to Guhāya. Salutation to Jyā. Salutation to the seat of Kṣetrapālaka. Salutation to the form of Kṣetrapālaka.

(4) He who bears matted locks of red flames, who wears the moon, whose body is composed of red radiance, who holds in his hands a trident, a skull-bowl, a noose, and a ḍamaru drum—the protector of the world. (5)
I salute the auspicious Kṣetrapāla Vaṭuka, the lord of spirits and piśācas, who is Nirvāṇa, whose vehicle is a dog, who has three eyes, and who is the source of the clamor of bliss.
(i.7a) Homage to Kṣetrapālaka! Jya! Homage to Viṣṇuvāsanā! Homage to Viṣṇumūrti! (2)
Viṣṇu has four arms, wears a garland, and holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
he resembles a dark blue cloud and is seated upon Garuḍa.
(3) Salutations to Viṣṇu. Salutations to the seat of Vīrabhadra. Salutations to the form of Vīrabhadra.
He is remembered as having four arms and three eyes, bestowing fearlessness and boons, and holding the deer and the axe. (4)

Adorned with a crown of matted locks and beautified by all ornaments—having meditated thus, one should worship the eight jars in succession, step by step. In the center of the northern altar: ... first, *namaḥ śyāmalāsanāya* (homage to the seat of Śyāmalā); *namaḥ śyāmalāmūrtaye* (homage to the form of Śyāmalā). (2)

Dark-complexioned, holding a lotus and nectar, with beautiful hands, adorned with divine garments, seated upon a lotus, granting boons and fearlessness, with a smiling face, and bearing a noose and a goad;
her right foot is bent and held by the left hand, while she stands with her left foot on the right [and her right foot on the left].
One should meditate upon Śrī Śyāmalā, who brings delight to the mind of Mannātha.

(4) *Namaḥ Śyāmalāya*. Having offered incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth, as well as water for the feet (*pādya*) and water for sipping (*ācamana*), and having performed the dedication of the recitation (*japa-samarpaṇa*), one should worship the power of the throne (*pīṭha-śakti*). In the northeast, starting from the base of the power, one should worship the eight *vardhanīs* in the east and other directions with their respective names:
*Ṛddhi* and *Buddhi* in the eastern part, and *Puṣkala* and *Pūrṇā* in the southeast. (2)
Having worshipped Vāgdevī in the south and Rudraśakti in the southwest;
The Guru should worship Vallī and Devasenā in the west;
Vāyuśakti in the northwest and Lakṣmīśakti in the north.

One should worship the Vīraśakti in the Īśāna [corner] and in the jars in due order: (4) *Oṃ, obeisance to the seat of Ṛddhi and Buddhi; obeisance to the form of Ṛddhi and Buddhi*. (5) She has two arms, possesses a yellow complexion, and her hands rest upon lotuses.
I bow to Ṛddhi and Buddhi on the right and left of Gaṇeśa.
(i.8b) Homage to Ṛddhi and Buddhi. Jya. Homage to the one seated upon the Puṣkalapūrṇa throne. Homage to the one whose form is Puṣkalapūrṇa.
Pūrṇā is remembered as having a golden luster, while Puṣkalā is dark-complexioned. (2)
She has two eyes and two arms, is gentle in appearance, and is adorned with all ornaments.
Her limbs were anointed with divine perfumes and she was adorned with celestial garlands and ointments;
(3) youthful, bearing weapons, full, abundant, and clad in golden garments;
(4) with a flower in her full left hand and a bracelet upon her right.

The left foot should be drawn up and the right one should hang down. (5) This is called the Siṃhakuṇḍala as well as the Makarakuṇḍala. She should hold a flower in her right hand and a flower in her left, and she should be in the Varada mudrā. (i.9a)
With the left foot hanging down and the right drawn up,
adorned with conch-shell earrings and likewise two lion-earrings—
having meditated thus in detail, one should worship with full offerings of flowers.
Salutation to Puṣkalapūrṇa. Jya. (3) Salutation to the one whose seat is Sarasvatī. Salutation to the form of Sarasvatī.
[He is] four-armed and two-eyed, white in color, and likewise clad in white garments;
in his right hand is a rosary of beads, and in his left hand a book. (4)
One should worship Sarasvatī, who is seated in the lotus posture, adorned with all ornaments, and endowed with all auspicious marks. (5)
Salutation to Sarasvatī. Having worshipped her: (I.9b) Salutation to the seat of Durgā; salutation to the form of Durgā.
[The goddess] is dark-complexioned, two-eyed, and endowed with four arms;
she is the goddess wearing white garments and adorned with all ornaments. (2)
One should meditate upon Viṣṇu-Durgā, who holds the conch, the discus, and the *ūrūhasta* [thigh-grasper], and who is seated upon Mahiṣa.
(3) Salutation to Durgā. *Jya*. Salutation to the seat of the army of gods (*devasenāsanāya*). Salutation to the form of the army of gods (*devasenāmūrtaye*). (4)
Yellow-hued, holding a blue lotus, the daughter of Śacī, adorned with divine garments;
with her left hand hanging down, the daughter of Mahendra wearing garlands of Mandāra flowers;
her sandals worshipped by the gods, moon-faced, standing to the left of the Commander of the Army. (5) (i.10a)
I worship the Goddess, adorned with various divine ornaments, possessing two eyes, and standing in the tribhaṅgī posture.
Salutation to Devasenānī! Salutation to Jyāvalyāsanā! Salutation to Valyāsanamūrti!

[I worship her] who is dark-complexioned, holding a lotus and nectar, radiant with jeweled earrings upon her ears, with a long garland hanging from her right side, adorned with a crown and tiara, possessing lofty breasts, and wearing a bodice.
One should meditate upon the Mistress of the Creeper (Vallīśvarī), who stands to the left of the one born from the Śara-forest, who is gazed upon by the army,
who wears a garland of Kuñja flowers, and whose eyes are like young sprouts.
Salutation to Valyā. (5) Salutation to the Seat of Īśvarī. Salutation to the Form of Īśvarī.
The Supreme Goddess should be dark-complexioned, two-eyed, two-armed, in the *tribhaṅgī* posture, with her right and left feet placed in a bent position;
she may hold a blue lotus in her right hand, be adorned with bracelets, and have her hands resting [on her knees].

Salutation to Īśvarī. (2) Salutation to the seat of Mahālakṣmī. Salutation to the form of Mahālakṣmī. I bow to Sindhu-lakṣmī, who holds a pair of lotuses with hands granting fearlessness and boons; who dwells upon a fresh lotus; who is adorned with jeweled earrings; (3) whose complexion resembles the dawn; who is Acyutā (the Imperishable); the mistress of the life of [Viṣṇu]; and who is worshipped by all the gods. (4)

Salutation to Mahālakṣmī. Salutation to the seat of Vīraśakti. Salutation to the form of Vīraśakti. One should meditate upon the goddess Vīraśakti, who has two arms and two eyes, who bestows fearlessness, who holds a lotus, and who is seated upon a lotus throne. (I.11a)
Salutation to Vīraśakti. Having performed the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and other rites as previously described, one should carry out the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) as prescribed.

(2) One should conceive the deity situated in the center of the fire as a three-part image (*trikhaṇḍa*), consisting of the nature of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva, preceded by the union of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*). (3)
One should install the Lords of the Principles (tattveśvara) and the Embodiments of the Principles (mūrtīśvara) in sequence;
specifically, one should install each section separately within every [part].
Having worshipped the Lords of the Principles in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should perform the fire-oblation (homa).
Having offered oblations to the embodied deities and their lords, one should subsequently perform the recitation according to the prescribed number.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the oblation, and the recitation for each section repeatedly,
one should then offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) that same night.
In the morning, having performed the expiatory oblation and other rites, the preceptor should extract the image;
having worshipped the pitcher as before, he should worship the image.
Having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths), [the deity] is established within the inner sanctum.
(4) One should perform the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and then join [the deity] into the fire-pot (*agnikumbha*).
(5) At an auspicious moment and a favorable planetary conjunction (*sulagna*), the preceptor (*deśika*) should lift the pots.
Having borne [the image] upon his head and circumambulated the temple,
he should then enter the inner sanctum for worship and consecration—
performing the consecration and offering according to the full extent of his means. (I.12a–2)
The wise man should honor all the Brahmins with ritual offerings,
along with the consecration of the patron amidst auspicious sounds.
The performer should worship the preceptor with garments, gold, ornaments, and other such gifts.
One should cause the preceptor and others to receive the entirety of one's possessions, such as the sacrificial fee and so forth.
The performer should feed the Brahmins and cause them to be honored with sacrificial gifts.
Thus ends the ritual for the installation of Manmatha and Śyāmalā in the *Sakalāgamasangraha*.
Homage to the Vināyaka of the Root of the Glorious Palmyra Tree.
But outside the Ālaya, all those frequented by sages are endowed with various forms and bear various names. (i.12b)
They wore sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, were adorned with matted hair and crowns,
were primarily devoted to the worship of Śiva, and were dedicated to the practice of yoga.
With faces made terrifying by fangs, bearing swords and shields,
cruel consumers of honey and meat, and devourers of *bhūtas* and *piśācas*—
these constantly attend upon him from all sides in the subterranean realm.
Homage to the Auspicious Vināyaka of the Tālamūla Root.

Oṃ hāṃ lūṃ, obeisance to Kṣmāmūrti. Oṃ hāṃ lūṃ, obeisance to Gaṇeśa, the lord of Kṣmāmūrti. (2) Oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to Vahnimūrti. Oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to Śāstṛ, the lord of Vahnimūrti. (3) Oṃ hāṃ śrūṃ, obeisance to Yajamānamūrti. Oṃ hāṃ śrūṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of Yajamānamūrti. (4)
Oṃ hāṃ ṣūṃ, obeisance to the Sun-form. Oṃ hāṃ ṣūṃ, obeisance to Rudra, the presiding lord of the Sun-form.
(5) Oṃ hāṃ vūṃ, obeisance to the Water-form. Oṃ hāṃ vūṃ, obeisance to Guha, the presiding lord of the Water-form.
(i.14a) Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the Wind-form. Oṃ hāṃ yūṃ, obeisance to Kṣetrapālaka, the presiding lord of the Wind-form. (2)

Oṃ hāṃ sūṃ, obeisance to the form of Indra. Oṃ hāṃ sūṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the presiding lord of the form of Indra. (3) Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the form of Kha. Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Vīrabhadra, the presiding lord of the form of Kha. The installation of Cāmuṇḍā. (i.14b)
Now I shall describe in detail, in due order, the installation of Cāmuṇḍā.

Having constructed and adorned a pavilion as previously described, and having performed the worship of Vighneśvara followed by the rite for an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should sprinkle the sacrificial hall and perform the worship of the Sun. Then, having offered the general water-offering (*sāmānyārghya*).

Having sprinkled the eastern door with the Astra-mantra and protected it with the Kavaca-mantra, [one should worship] in the middle of the archway (*toraṇa*): Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to the Peaceful Archway (*śāntitoraṇa*). Obeisance to Bhadra, the lord of the Peaceful Archway. Obeisance to the Ṛgveda. Obeisance to the Kṛtayuga. At the trident: obeisance to Gaṅgā; obeisance to Mahālakṣmī; obeisance to Narmadā. On the northern banner of the door: obeisance to Praśānta. On the southern banner: obeisance to Śiśira. At the upper *udumbara* beam: obeisance to Gaṇapati.

Sarasvatī. (i.15a) Salutation to Mahālakṣmī. On the southern and northern door-posts: salutation to Nandin; salutation to Kuṇḍaliśakti; salutation to Mahākāla; salutation to Pādaniśakti; salutation to Indra; salutation to Dehiniśakti. At the lower part of the door-post: Oṃ Hrīṃ Aḥ, salutation to the Astra weapon and the Door-guardian. (3) Salutation to the *avarga*; salutation to the *kavarga*. On the banner situated above the door: salutation to Soma; salutation to Budha. On the Agni-banner: (4) salutation to Agni; salutation to Svāhādevī.

Having sprinkled the southern gate with the Astra-mantra: *Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Bhūti archway*. (5) Obeisance to Vijaya, the lord of the Bhūti archway; obeisance to the Yajurveda; obeisance to the Tretā Yuga; obeisance to Yamunā; (6) obeisance to Sarasvatī; obeisance to Mahālakṣmī. On the eastern and western branches: obeisance to Bhṛṅgin; obeisance to the Hlādinī Śakti. (i.15b) *Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Vināyaka*; obeisance to Vallabha; obeisance to Yama; obeisance to Kālakaṇṭhī.

At the lower *dumbara* pillar: "Obeisance to the weapon-gatekeeper. (2) Obeisance to the *ca*-group. Obeisance to the *ṭa*-group. On the banner situated above the door: "Obeisance to Bṛhaspati; obeisance to Bhārgava. On the banner in the southwest corner (*naiṛtikoṇa*): "Obeisance to Nṛti; obeisance to Dehini-śakti; obeisance to Viṣṇu; obeisance to Mahālakṣmī; obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the site (*vāstvadhipati*). (4) *Jya*. Having sprinkled the western door with the weapon-mantra: "Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the strength-gate (*balatoraṇa*)."

Homage to Vajra, the lord of the eastern archway. On the two branches of the archway: homage to the Sāmaveda; homage to the Dvāpara Yuga; homage to Godāvarī; homage to Umā; homage to Kāverī. On the southern banner: homage to Bhūtasañjīvana. On the northern banner: homage to Amṛtasañjīvana. On the upper *udumbara* beam: homage to Gaṇapati, Sarasvatī, and Lakṣmī. On the southern and northern branches: homage to Vṛṣabha; homage to Bhadra.

(2) Salutation to Smṛti. Salutation to Śacīsuta. Salutation to Varuṇa. Salutation to Vāriṇī. At the lower *dumbara* [pillar]: salutation to the door-guardian Astra. Salutation to the Tavarga. (3) Salutation to the Pavarga. Salutation to Aṅgāraka. Salutation to Śainaiścara. At the banner in the northwest corner: salutation to Vāyu. Salutation to Ghorashakti. Salutation to Gaṇapati. Salutation to Vallabha. Salutation to Mahālakṣmī. Jya.

Having sprinkled the northern gate with the Astra-mantra: *Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Ārogya archway; obeisance to Nīlalohita, the lord of the Ārogya archway; obeisance to the Atharvaveda; obeisance to the Kali Yuga; obeisance to Śaubhadra on the trident; obeisance to Bhāgīrathī; obeisance to Tuṅgabhadra.* On the western door-banner: obeisance to Dhanada. On the eastern banner: obeisance to Śrīprada.

On the eastern *udumbara* post: salutations to Gaṇapati, Sarasvatī, and Mahālakṣmī. On the western and eastern branches: salutations to the Goddess; salutations to Caṇḍeśvara; salutations to Rūpiṇī; salutations to Bhūtaniśakti; salutations to Kubera. On the lower *udumbara* post: salutations to the Weapon, the Guardian of the Door; salutations to the *Ya*-group; salutations to the *Śa*-group. On the banner situated above the door: salutations to Rāhu; salutations to Ketu. On the banner in the northeast corner: salutations to Īśāna.

(i.17a) Salutation to Harṣaṇāśakti. Salutation to Brahmā. Salutation to Sarasvatī. Salutation to the seven Gurus. JYA. At the northern *vardhanī* of the eastern gate: (2) Oṃ hyaiṃ (2) salutation to the seat of Śāntikalā. Oṃ hrīṃ salutation to the seat of Jayā. At the southern *vardhanī* of the gate: hrīṃ salutation to the seat of Vijayā. JYA. (3)

On the eastern *vardhanī* of the southern gate: *sa-hrīṃ vidyākalāya namaḥ*. On its eastern *vardhanī*: *hrīṃ yoginyāsanāya namaḥ*. (4) On the western *vardhanī* of the door: *hrīṃ mohinyāsanāya namaḥ*.

On the southern *vardhanī* of the western gate: *oṃ hrīṃ nivṛttikalāsanāya namaḥ*. (5) On its southern *vardhanī*: *malinyāsanāya namaḥ*. On the northern *vardhanī* of the door: *mālinyāsanāya namaḥ*. (i.17b)

On the western *vardhanī* of the northern gate: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the seat of the *pratiṣṭhā*-kalā. Jya. On its western *vardhanī*: hrīṃ, obeisance to the seat of Bhoginī. (2) On the eastern *vardhanī* of the [northern] gate: hrīṃ, obeisance to the seat of Bhogavatī. Jya.

In the middle of the sky—*namaḥ śāntyatītakalāyai*. Having looked with the vision of reality (*tattvadṛṣṭyā*), having struck the remaining doors, having worshipped the door-keepers as if they were permanent, and having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth; having donned the sacred thread, garments, crown, and other ornaments; having scattered the *vikira* offerings as before; having worshipped Brahmā in the southwest; and having worshipped Mahālakṣmī with *hrīṃ mahālakṣmyai namaḥ* at the southern water-vessel of Vāyu; one should worship Yāgeśvara upon his movable seat.

In the northern corner of the Sun: *Oṃ* (jya), salutation to the seat of Brāhmī. In the southeastern corner: *Oṃ* (jya), salutation to the seat of Māheśvarī. In the southern [corner]: *Oṃ* (jya), salutation to the seat of Kaumārī. In the southwestern corner: *Oṃ* (jya), salutation to the seat of Vaiṣṇavī. In the western [corner]: *Oṃ* (jya), salutation to the seat of Vārāhī. In the northwestern corner: *Oṃ* (jya), salutation to the seat of Māhendrī. In the northern [corner]: *Oṃ* (jya), salutation to the seat of Cāmuṇḍā. In the northeastern corner: *Oṃ* (jya), salutation to the seat of Śivadurgā.

To the south of Īśāna—(4) *namaḥ* to the seat of Sarasvatī. *Jya*. To the north of Nairṛti—*namaḥ* to the seat of Mahālakṣmī. *Jya*. In the directions beginning with Indra, one should worship the ten weapons: *Huṃ phaṭ namaḥ* to the sword. *Huṃ phaṭ namaḥ* to the skull-bowl. *Huṃ phaṭ namaḥ* to the bell. *Huṃ phaṭ namaḥ* to the iron arrow (*nārāca*). *Huṃ phaṭ namaḥ* to the hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*). *Huṃ phaṭ namaḥ* to the banner. *Huṃ phaṭ namaḥ* to the razor. *Huṃ phaṭ namaḥ* to the noose. *Huṃ phaṭ namaḥ* to the lotus. *Huṃ phaṭ namaḥ* to the discus. *Jya*.
O Brahmī, by your command, Cāmuṇḍā shall remain with vigilance until the end of the sacrifice for the sake of pacifying obstacles in your own abode.

Thereafter—just as in the *Śivapratiṣṭhā*—having taken up the *Vardhanī* vessel as before and having worshipped [the deities] from the *Ādhāraśakti* up to the end of the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) while seated on a firm seat; first, in the eastern jar: *Oṃ vighnavināyakāsanāya namaḥ*. To its east: *Kṣetrapālakāsanāya namaḥ*. To its east: *Ratnajvālāsanāya namaḥ*. In the northeast: *Paścime paraśurāmāsanāya namaḥ*.
[He is] adorned with a crown and earrings, two-legged, and two-armed.
I do not resort to the pleasure of the mouth, which holds a bow and arrows in its hand.
A hero, a great hero among heroes, bearing weapons in the form of a blow;
adorned with a garland of skulls, with hair standing erect and prominent fangs.

Salutations to Paraśurāma. Having worshipped Dharma and the other [guardians] at the four pillars of the altar (*vedī*), one should worship the twelve Ādityas upon the twelve pillars. On the altar: *Oṃ hrīṃ, salutations to the Earth element*. On the pillars: *Salutations to the Water element*. On the hands [of the pillars]: *Salutations to the Fire element*. On the beams: *Salutations to the Air element*. On the grass: *Salutations to the Space element*. On the canopies: *Salutations to the Moon*. On the ripples: *Salutations to Jāhnavī*.
(3) In the mirrors—salutation to Sūrya. In the garland of *darbha* grass—salutation to Vāsukī.

In the space between the altars—among the eight auspicious symbols (*maṅgala*) situated in the eight directions starting from the east: On the elephant held by Urvaśī: *Obeisance to Indra, the lord of elephants.* On the full vessel held by Menakā: *Obeisance to Jaleśvara, the lord of the full vessel.* On the banner held by Rambhā: *Obeisance to Cāmuṇḍā, the lord of the banner.* On the lamp held by Kāmavardhanī: *Obeisance to Agnijihva, the lord of the lamp.* On the pair of chowries held by Tilottamā: *Obeisance to Mātariśvan, the lord of the pair of chowries.*

To the one holding a conch, Kāmukhī—homage to Vimala, the Lord of the Conch. To the one holding a lotus, Kāmavardhanī—homage to Candra, the Lord of the Lotus. To the one holding a svastika, Sundarī—homage to Raudrī, the Lord of the Svastika. From Ādhāraśakti up to Padmā: homage to Karālī of the East; homage to Vikarālī; homage to Bhadrakālī; homage to Mahādevī; homage to Mahāraudrī; homage to Mahāśūlī; homage to Manonmanī.

Salutation to Mahāśakti. (2) [In the pericarp... Salutation to Sarasvatī. Salutation to the solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*). Salutation to Brahmiṇī, the sovereign of the solar disc. (3) Salutation to the lunar disc (*somamaṇḍala*). Salutation to Vaiṣṇavī, the sovereign of the lunar disc. Salutation to the fiery disc (*vahnimaṇḍala*). (4) Salutation to Raudrī, the sovereign of the fiery disc. Salutation to the disc of power (*śaktimaṇḍala*). Salutation to Cāmuṇḍā, the sovereign of the disc of power. Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the seat of Cāmuṇḍā. (5)

Salutation to the form of Cāmuṇḍā. In this form, [one should place the mantras] on the head, face, heart, private parts, feet, and all other limbs: On the head: *oṃ sem īśānamūrdhāya namaḥ*. On the face: *oṃ seṃ tatpuruṣavaktrāya namaḥ*. On the heart: *oṃ sūṃ aghorahṛdayāya namaḥ*. On the private parts: *oṃ sīṃ vāmadevaguhyāya namaḥ*. On the form of the feet: *oṃ saṃ sadyojātamūrtaye namaḥ*. The sequence for the staff (*daṇḍabhaṅgī*): On the head: *oṃ hrīṃ raktacāmuṇḍāyai namaḥ*. On the face: *oṃ hrīṃ mahācāmuṇḍāyai namaḥ*. In the eyes: *oṃ hrīṃ medhāyai namaḥ*. In the eyes: *oṃ hrīṃ kālyai namaḥ*.

In the nose: *oṃ hrīṃ kalāyai namaḥ*. In the two lips: *oṃ hrīṃ kāmarūpiṇyai namaḥ*. In the throat: *oṃ hrīṃ raktyai namaḥ*. In the heart: *oṃ hrīṃ kāmavardhanyai namaḥ*. In the belly: *oṃ hrīṃ pañcamukhyai namaḥ*. In the navel: *oṃ hrīṃ khaḍgahastāyai namaḥ*. In the left hand: *oṃ hrīṃ ḍamarukahastāyai namaḥ*. In the right hand: *oṃ hrīṃ sarasvatyai namaḥ*.

(2) On the vulva: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Kapālinī. On the left thigh: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Kālakaṇṭhī. On the right thigh: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Mahāmāyā. (3) On the left knee: obeisance to Ūrdhvakeśinī. On the right knee: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Mohinī. On the left shank: Oṃ (4) hrīṃ, obeisance to Kālinī. On the right shank: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Tārā. On the left foot: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Vidyā.

On the right foot: *oṃ hrīṃ grāmarakṣāyai namaḥ*. On the left hand: *oṃ hrīṃ niśīthinyai namaḥ*. On the right hand: *oṃ hrīṃ mālinyai namaḥ*. On the left side: *oṃ hrīṃ prabhāvatyai namaḥ*. On the right side: *oṃ hrīṃ daṃṣṭrākarālinyai namaḥ*. In the upper portion: *oṃ hrīṃ piṅgalākṣyai namaḥ*. In the lower portion: [oṃ hrīṃ...]. Having thus performed the deposition (*nyāsa*) of the twenty-six digits (*kalā*) with their respective mudrās and so forth, the meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
Having four arms, three eyes, and endowed with two feet;
with hair standing erect, excellent fangs, and possessed of a fierce gaze;
with the right foot hanging down and the left foot resting upon a corpse.
In her right hands she holds a joined ḍamaru drum and a noose;
in the upper left hands she holds a trident and a skull-cup.
She is blue in color, of magnificent form, and laughs with eight faces from her left foot.
With long lips, eyes like mātulaṅga fruits, and endowed with great fangs,
Cāmuṇḍā is described as having a fierce form and a majestic appearance.

Oṃ hrāṃ hrauṃ, obeisance to the one whose body is knowledge (*vidyādeha*). (3) Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the eyes. Having filled the hollowed palms with flowers: Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ haiṃ, to Cāmuṇḍinī (4) and Raktacāmuṇḍā, slay, slay! burn, burn! Oṃ phaṭ svāhā! (5) Having performed the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*), stabilization (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), and confinement (*sannirodhana*), and having offered the water of confinement (*nirodhārghya*), one should address [the deity] thus: "O Goddess, Sovereign of the Entire World, until the conclusion of the worship, may you remain present within this vessel with a spirit of affection. (i.23a) Thus, one should make the request.

Having offered a welcome and the *arghya* water, one should perform the placement [of mantras] at the locations from the heart to the ends of the hands: *oṃ hrāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hrīṃ śirase namaḥ*; *oṃ hrūṃ śikhāyai vauṣaṭ*; *oṃ hraiṃ kavacāya huṃ*; *oṃ hauṃ netrebhyo vauṣaṭ*; *oṃ haḥ astrāya phaṭ*. Having established oneness with the root mantra, having protected with the weapon mantra, having shielded with the armor mantra, having rendered it nectar with the *dhenumudrā*, having displayed the *trikhaṇḍayonimudrā*, and having shown the *mahāmudrā*.

Having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*), and having performed a mental consecration (*mānasābhiṣeka*) and adorned [the deity] with sandalwood, saffron, and other substances: *Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to Cāmuṇḍā, the sovereign of the *ātmatattva*. Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to Cāmuṇḍā, the sovereign of the *vidyātattva*. Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to Cāmuṇḍā, the sovereign of the *śivatattva*.

The limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*): (3) *Oṃ hrāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*—on the petal in the southeast; *śirase namaḥ*—on the petal in the northeast; *hrūṃ śikhāyai namaḥ*—on the petal in the southwest; *kavacāya hūṃ*—on the petal in the northwest; *astrāya phaṭ*—in the four directions starting from the east. One should contemplate the oneness of all these with Cāmuṇḍā. (I.24a) Then, in the second enclosure, in the corners starting from the east: *Oṃ hrīṃ vāmāsanāya namaḥ*; *vāmamūrtaye namaḥ*.
And [one should visualize] Vāma, blue in luster and adorned with a crown and other ornaments. (2)
I worship the Goddess who bears the conch and the discus, facing toward the Goddess.
Salutation to Vāmā. Jya. (3) Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the seat of Jyeṣṭhā; salutation to the form of Jyeṣṭhā.
I worship Jyeṣṭhā, who is yellow in luster, holding a lotus in her hand, adorned with all ornaments, wearing white garments, and facing the Goddess. (4)
Salutation to Jyeṣṭhā. Jya. Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to Raudryāsanā. Salutation to the form of Raudrī.
I worship the goddess Raudrī, who has the luster of a blue color, possesses three eyes, holds a trident, is adorned with a crown of matted hair, and faces toward the Goddess. (I.24b)
Salutation to Raudrī. Jya. Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the seat of Kālī. (2) Salutation to the form of Kālī.
One should worship the goddess facing the [main] deity—Kālī, who resembles a dark cloud, who holds a spear and a mallet, and who possesses a formidable countenance. (3)

Salutation to Kālī. Jya. Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the seat of Kalavikaraṇī; salutation to the form of Kalavikaraṇī. One should worship her who has a reddish luster and a white face, who holds a noose in her hand and possesses great strength, who is adorned with a crown and a diadem, and who faces the Goddess.

Salutation to Kalavikaraṇī. Jya. (I.25a) Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the seat of Balavikaraṇā; salutation to the form of Balavikaraṇā. One should worship the goddess Agnimukhī, who is yellow in luster, wears yellow garments, holds a sword and a shield, and is adorned with all ornaments.
*Balavikaraṇyai namaḥ*. *Jya*. Oṃ Hrīṃ (3). *Balapramathanī-āsanāya namaḥ*. *Balapramathanī-mūrtaye namaḥ*.
One should worship the fierce goddess Balapramathanī, who possesses a luster like blue collyrium, who holds a staff and the gesture of fearlessness, and who faces the Goddess. (4)

Salutation to Balapramathinī. Jya. Oṃ (5) Hrīṃ, salutation to the seat of Sarvabhūtadamani; salutation to the form of Sarvabhūtadamani. One should worship the goddesses facing [the practitioner]: she who is called Sarvabhūtadamani, who is green in color, in the full bloom of youth, holding a spear in her hand, possessed of great heroism, and facing the deities. (i.25b)
Salutation to the subduers of all beings.

*Jya*. (2) In the third enclosure: Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to Jayā; salutation to Vijayā; salutation to Yoginī; salutation to Mohinī; salutation to Malinī; salutation to Mālinī; (3) salutation to Bhoginī; salutation to Bhogavatī. *Jya*.

The fourth enclosure: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Brāhmī; obeisance to Māheśvarī; (4) obeisance to Kaumārī; obeisance to Vaiṣṇavī; obeisance to Vārāhī; obeisance to Cāmuṇḍā; obeisance to Śivadurgā; obeisance to Sarasvatī; (5) obeisance to Mahālakṣmī. Jya. In the fifth enclosure—

Oṃ hrīṃ khaḍgāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ hrīṃ kapālāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ | (i.26a) Oṃ hrīṃ ghaṇṭāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ hrīṃ nārācāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ hrīṃ ḍamarukāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ hrīṃ dhvajāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ hrīṃ kṣurikāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ hrīṃ pāśāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ hrīṃ padmāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ hrīṃ cakrāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Having performed the recitation (*japa*) of the bowstring, incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth, one should pray to the Goddess.

Afterwards, [he should perform] up to the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) according to the procedure stated for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*). Having worshipped Cāmuṇḍā within the fire—from the Foundation Power (*ādhāraśakti*) up to the fifth enclosure—he effects a union between the mouth of Cāmuṇḍā and the mouth of the fire. Having emerged [from her], he recites the root mantra of Cāmuṇḍā. He should meditate on the flame of light in the form of a crest, which has issued from the nose of Cāmuṇḍā residing in the fire and has merged with the crest of Śiva residing in the sacrificial ground; it is uninterrupted by being separated from mere rays, and it has established its seat in both places.

(4) Having performed the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*), and for the sake of that joining, having offered three oblations with the root mantra; for the sake of satiating the mantra, having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra of Cāmuṇḍā; and for the sake of special satiation, having offered one hundred and eight oblations; having performed the kindling of the satiation, and according to the requirements of the substance and the time, having offered one hundred oblations with the weapon-mantra (*astra*); [the materials are: sacrificial wood (*samit*), clarified butter (*ājya*), sacrificial porridge (*caru*), parched grain (*lāja*), barley meal (*saktu*), mustard seed (*sarṣapa*), sesame (*tila*), green gram (*mudga*), jaggery (*guḍa*), bamboo, grain, and *priyaṅgu*. (2)
Honey, milk, and curd—these fifteen substances are prescribed;
one should strike them in due order with the Reṇugāyatrī mantra.
Having offered the *vyāhṛti* at the end of each substance, and with a full oblation for every substance—
thus ends the chapter on the ritual procedure for the worship of Cāmuṇḍā in the great tantra called Raurava.
Salutation to the Vināyaka of the Root of the Glorious Palmyra Tree.
Homage to the Lord Guru.

(i.27b) Oṃ hāṃ lūṃ, homage to Kṣmāmūrti. Oṃ hāṃ lūṃ, homage to Vāmā, the presiding deity of Kṣmāmūrti. (2) Oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ, homage to Vahnimūrti. Oṃ hāṃ hrīṃ, homage to Jyeṣṭhā, the presiding deity of Vahnimūrti. (3) Oṃ hāṃ śūṃ, homage to Yajamānamūrti. Oṃ hāṃ hrīṃ, homage to Raudrī, the presiding deity of Yajamānamūrti. (4) Oṃ hāṃ ṣūṃ, homage to Arkamūrti.

Oṃ hāṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Kālī, the sovereign of the solar form. (5) Oṃ hāṃ vūṃ, obeisance to the watery form. Oṃ hāṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Kalavikaraṇī, the sovereign of the watery form. (i.28a) Oṃ hāṃ yūṃ, obeisance to the airy form. Oṃ hāṃ yūṃ, obeisance to Balavikaraṇī, the sovereign of the airy form. (2) Oṃ hāṃ sūṃ, obeisance to the lunar form. Oṃ hāṃ sūṃ, obeisance to Balapramathanī, the sovereign of the lunar form.
(3) Oṃ hāṃ huṃ, homage to Khamūrti. Oṃ hāṃ huṃ, homage to Khamūrtyadhipā, the subduer of all beings.
